title: Breathing trial in an older patient after surgery
summary: A 79-year-old man has been breathing on minimal support for 20 minutes after abdominal surgery.
rationale: An older patient with reduced reserve but adequate drive still passes: RSBI stays well under 105 on PS 5/PEEP 5, so prompt extubation is right; sedation removes his own breathing, so the apnoea alarm sounds and the ventilator apnoea backup (RR 12) breathes for him: gases hold, but the trial is lost and extubation is delayed. Headless engine check on the starting settings and after the named actions: untouched by 5 min: PaCO2 39, pH 7.41, SpO2 98%, Pplat 15, RSBI 48, RR 19, SBP 137; untouched by 40 min: PaCO2 39, pH 7.41, SpO2 98%, Pplat 15, RSBI 44, RR 18, SBP 137; typical mistake by 40 min: PaCO2 40, pH 7.39, SpO2 98%, Pplat 20, RSBI 4, RR 12, SBP 137. Values for an arm whose case ended early (improved or deteriorated trigger) are the values when it ended.

retestsMistake.clinicalFocus: Age alone is not a reason to fail an SBT: rely on RSBI, gas exchange and work of breathing; sedation would remove the drive that makes him pass

source: The Ventilator Book 3e (weaning / SBT chapter, number unverified); Marino ICU Book 2025 (liberation from mechanical ventilation chapter, unverified); Nunn & Lumb 9e (control of breathing / respiratory muscle chapter, unverified); Boles JM, et al. Weaning from mechanical ventilation. Eur Respir J 2007;29:1033-56; Yang KL, Tobin MJ. N Engl J Med 1991;324:1445-50 (RSBI below 105). Compliance 40 and reserve 0.5 are teaching assumptions (unverified).

changes.vignette: Male 79, 172 cm, 74 kg. PSV 5 / PEEP 5, FiO2 0.3, trial 20 minutes.

patient.presentingStory: Day 3 after laparotomy for a perforated diverticulum. Awake, following commands, afebrile, secretions minimal. On a spontaneous breathing trial, PS 5 / PEEP 5, FiO2 0.3 for 20 minutes. The nurse is worried that "he is 79" and asks whether to give a little sedation to keep him comfortable.
patient.history: Hypertension, mild CKD. Independent at home. Full escalation.

then.detail: Extubated before completing a 30-minute spontaneous breathing trial. Even when the first minutes look good, finish the trial.

then.reason: Extubated before the trial was complete. He did well, but the decision was made too early.

then.text: The endotracheal tube is smoothly removed after airway suctioning and cuff deflation. The patient is placed on 2 L/min nasal cannula, breathing comfortably with a clear voice and no stridor.

then.reason: Patient successfully extubated to nasal cannula following a passed spontaneous breathing trial with stable gas exchange, low RSBI, and preserved respiratory muscle endurance.

then.text: The patient has maintained comfortable spontaneous breathing with stable vitals, normal RSBI, and low fatigue for over 30 minutes on minimal support. Are we ready to extubate?

then.detail: Administering sedation to a patient undergoing a successful spontaneous breathing trial suppresses respiratory drive: he stops breathing for himself, the ventilator apnoea backup takes over, and the trial and extubation are delayed.

then.reason: Sedation abolished spontaneous breathing during the trial. The ventilator apnoea backup took over, so he is not in danger, but the trial is lost and extubation is delayed.
The trial was passed but the patient was left intubated. Every extra day on the ventilator carries risk.

actions.text: Sedation administered. The patient has become unarousable; spontaneous respiratory drive is suppressed and low minute ventilation alarms are sounding.

orderEffects.note: Sedative administration blunts respiratory drive and arrests the spontaneous breathing trial

predictionPoints.question: Which set of findings indicates that this patient has successfully passed his spontaneous breathing trial and is physiologically ready for extubation consideration?
options: RSBI < 105 bpm/L, spontaneous RR 16-22 bpm, stable gas exchange without respiratory distress or fatigue
RSBI > 150 bpm/L with rapid shallow breathing and tachypnoea
Complete absence of spontaneous breathing efforts requiring mandatory ventilation
Minute ventilation > 20 L/min driven by heavy scalene accessory muscle recruitment
predictionPoints.answerKey: RSBI < 105 bpm/L, spontaneous RR 16-22 bpm, stable gas exchange without respiratory distress or fatigue
predictionPoints.explanation: Passing criteria for an SBT include an RSBI < 105 breaths/min/L, spontaneous respiratory rate < 35 bpm, absence of hemodynamic instability, acceptable oxygenation/acid-base status, and lack of subjective distress or diaphoresis (Yang & Tobin 1991; ATS/ACCP Liberation Guidelines 2017).

predictionPoints.question: Having successfully passed a spontaneous breathing trial with RSBI ~40 bpm/L, normal gas exchange, and minimal secretions, what is the recommended next step?
options: Proceed with extubation to supplemental oxygen (e.g. low-flow nasal cannula)
Place the patient back on full assist-control ventilation for 48 hours of rest
Initiate continuous deep sedation with propofol infusion
Increase pressure support to 20 cmH2O and perform recruitment manoeuvres
predictionPoints.answerKey: Proceed with extubation to supplemental oxygen (e.g. low-flow nasal cannula)
predictionPoints.explanation: According to ATS/ACCP 2017 guidelines, patients who pass an SBT should be considered promptly for extubation unless there are specific airway contraindications. Unnecessary prolongation of intubation increases the risk of ventilator-associated pneumonia and laryngeal trauma.

rubric.description: Examined patient and assessed clinical stability during spontaneous breathing trial
Checked arterial blood gas during SBT to verify adequate alveolar ventilation and oxygenation
Maintained rapid shallow breathing index (RSBI) < 105 and low fatigue (< 0.25) during the trial
Extubated after the 30-minute trial was complete, once it had clearly been passed (by minute 45)
Avoided sedating patient during spontaneous breathing trial

keyPoints: A spontaneous breathing trial (SBT) on low pressure support (e.g. PS 5 cmH2O, PEEP 5 cmH2O) assesses whether the patient can sustain the work of breathing independently.

A passed SBT is characterized by stable respiratory rate (< 35 bpm, typically 16-22 bpm), preserved tidal volume (400-500 mL), RSBI < 105 bpm/L (typically 35-55 bpm/L), low fatigue (< 0.25), and stable oxygenation and hemodynamics.
Once SBT passing criteria are met and airway reflexes/secretions are manageable, extubation should be performed promptly to avoid ventilator-associated complications.

Clinical Caveat: RSBI measured on PSV is typically 20-40% lower than on a T-piece due to pressure unloading. In addition to RSBI < 105 bpm/L, successful extubation requires confirmed airway protection, cough strength, and manageable secretions (cuff leak test if laryngeal edema risk exists).
Administering sedation during an SBT suppresses central respiratory drive and induces iatrogenic hypoventilation.
An RSBI below 105 was validated on unsupported breathing; on pressure support a stricter cut-off (about 80) is sensible.
